This article works through one analysis from start to end: the model, the
data, specifying and fitting a model, reading the results, adding a covariate
and checking the model. It assumes ctsem and its Julia engine are installed,
as the README describes.

```{r libs}
library(ctsem)
library(ggplot2)
```

# The model

A ctsem model describes one or more latent processes that change over time,
and the variables measured at the times they were observed. Within each
subject the processes $\boldsymbol\eta(t)$ follow

$$
\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol\eta(t) = \big(A\,\boldsymbol\eta(t) + \mathbf b + M\boldsymbol\chi(t)\big)\,\mathrm{d}t + G\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf W(t)
$$

and the measurements are

$$
\mathbf y(t) = \Lambda\,\boldsymbol\eta(t) + \boldsymbol\tau + \boldsymbol\epsilon(t),
\qquad \boldsymbol\epsilon(t) \sim N(\mathbf 0, \Theta)
$$

Each symbol is a matrix of `ctModel()`:

| Matrix | Symbol | Holds | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| `DRIFT` | $A$ | auto effects (diagonal) and cross effects between processes | free |
| `CINT` | $\mathbf b$ | continuous time intercepts | zero |
| `DIFFUSION` | $G$ | size and correlation of the random shocks to the processes | free |
| `TDPREDEFFECT` | $M$ | effects of time dependent predictors $\boldsymbol\chi$ | free |
| `T0MEANS` | | the processes' values at each subject's first observation | free, varying over subjects |
| `T0VAR` | | their variance at the first observation | covered by the random `T0MEANS` |
| `LAMBDA` | $\Lambda$ | loadings of the measured variables on the processes | must be given |
| `MANIFESTMEANS` | $\boldsymbol\tau$ | intercepts of the measured variables | free, varying over subjects |
| `MANIFESTVAR` | $\Theta$ | measurement error | free standard deviations |

The drift matrix describes how the processes change. With a negative auto
effect, a process on its own returns towards its equilibrium after a shock. A
cross effect is the effect of one process on the rate of change of another.
Whether the processes together return to equilibrium depends on the whole
drift matrix, which `vignette('dynamics')` explains. The diffusion describes
the random shocks that move the processes between observations, and so carry
forward in time. Measurement error affects only the observation it belongs
to. A time dependent predictor, such as an intervention, shifts the processes
at the times it is observed, and the dynamics carry the shift forward.

Any parameter can differ between subjects, as a random effect, and depend on
subject level covariates (time independent predictors). By default the
initial states and the intercepts of the measured variables differ between
subjects, which allows for stable differences between people.

With `type = 'dt'` the same matrices describe a discrete time model, in which
`DRIFT` holds the autoregressive and cross-lagged coefficients from one
occasion to the next.

# Data

ctsem takes data in long format: one row per subject and occasion, with a
column for the subject id, one for the time, and one for each measured
variable and predictor.

- Times are numbers, in whatever unit suits the processes, such as hours, days
  or years. They need not be equally spaced and can differ between subjects.
  The estimated effects are per unit of time, so the unit decides their scale.
  A unit over which the processes change noticeably, but do not settle
  completely, usually works best.
- A missing value is `NA`. A row can have some variables observed and others
  missing.
- A time independent predictor must have the same value on every row of a
  subject.
- A time dependent predictor is an input at the time of its row, and zero
  means no input.

The data for this article are simulated, so that the estimates can be
compared with the values that generated them. One hundred people rated their
stress and mood about once a day, at irregular times, for a month or so, and
some ratings are missing. In the generating model stress lowers mood but mood
does not affect stress, each person has their own typical stress and mood,
and older people tend to be more stressed. `age` is standardised.

```{r simulate}
set.seed(1)
gen <- ctModel(type = 'ct', silent = TRUE,
  manifestNames = c('stress', 'mood'), latentNames = c('stress', 'mood'),
  LAMBDA = diag(2), TIpredNames = 'age',
  DRIFT = matrix(c(-0.5, 0, -0.25, -0.3), 2, 2, byrow = TRUE),
  DIFFUSION = matrix(c(0.8, 0, 0, 0.6), 2, 2, byrow = TRUE),
  CINT = matrix(0, 2, 1), T0MEANS = matrix(0, 2, 1), T0VAR = diag(1, 2),
  MANIFESTMEANS = matrix(c('mm_stress|param|TRUE|0.5|age=0.3',
    'mm_mood|param|TRUE|0.5'), 2, 1),
  MANIFESTVAR = diag(0.4, 2))
dat <- ctGenerate(gen, n = 100, Tpoints = 30, dtmean = 1, logdtsd = 0.5,
  backend = 'julia', values = c(mm_stress = 3, mm_mood = 5))
truelevels <- attr(dat, 'subjectpars')
dat <- data.frame(dat)
dat$time <- round(dat$time, 2)
dat$stress[sample(nrow(dat), 200)] <- NA
dat$mood[sample(nrow(dat), 200)] <- NA
head(dat)
```

```{r plotdata, fig.height = 3.5}
long <- rbind(
  data.frame(dat[dat$id <= 3, c('id', 'time')], variable = 'stress',
    value = dat$stress[dat$id <= 3]),
  data.frame(dat[dat$id <= 3, c('id', 'time')], variable = 'mood',
    value = dat$mood[dat$id <= 3]))
ggplot(long[!is.na(long$value), ], aes(time, value, colour = variable)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1) + facet_wrap(~id, labeller = label_both) +
  theme_bw() + labs(x = 'time (days)', y = NULL)
```

Data in wide format, with one row per subject, can be converted.
`ctWideToLong()` gives one row per occasion, and `ctDeintervalise()` turns
the time intervals of wide data into times:

```{r wide}
data(ctExample1)
colnames(ctExample1)
widelong <- ctWideToLong(ctExample1, Tpoints = 6, n.manifest = 2,
  manifestNames = c('LeisureTime', 'Happiness'))
widelong <- data.frame(ctDeintervalise(widelong))
head(widelong)
```

# Specifying the model

Each process is measured by one variable, with a loading of 1, so `LAMBDA` is
an identity matrix. `ctModel()` takes the names of the time and id columns from
its `time` and `id` arguments, which default to `'time'` and `'id'`.

```{r model}
model <- ctModel(LAMBDA = diag(2),
  manifestNames = c('stress', 'mood'), latentNames = c('stress', 'mood'))
model
```

Printing the model shows each matrix, with the name of each free parameter
and the value of each fixed one. Everything not given to `ctModel()` takes the
defaults in the table above. `ctModelLatex(model)` writes the same model as
equations, and opens them as a pdf if LaTeX is installed:

```{r latex-model, echo = FALSE, out.width = '100%'}
latexFigure(model)
```

The first line is the distribution of the random effects: each person's
starting values and measurement intercepts are drawn from a normal
distribution, on the raw scale of the parameters, and then transformed. The
next two lines are the dynamics, the two after them the measurement, and the
last line the distribution of the random shocks over an interval.

To change a matrix, give it to `ctModel()`. A
number fixes a cell, and a name estimates it. This drift matrix would fix the
effect of mood on stress at zero:

```{r model-fixed, eval = FALSE}
DRIFT = matrix(c('drift_stress',      0,
                 'drift_mood_stress', 'drift_mood'), 2, 2, byrow = TRUE)
```

The same model can be written in lavaan, Mplus or formula syntax, which
`vignette('model-syntax')` describes.

# Fitting

```{r fit}
fit <- ctFit(dat, model, cores = 2)
```

By default `ctFit()` finds the maximum likelihood estimates, integrating over
the latent states and over the differences between people. `cores` sets the
number of CPU cores to use. `priors = TRUE` adds weakly informative priors,
which helps with small data sets, and `optimize = FALSE` samples the
posterior instead of optimising. `vignette('uncertainty')` compares these.

# Reading the results

`summary(fit)` prints every part of the result. The population values of the
parameters are in `popmeans`:

```{r popmeans}
s <- summary(fit)
s$popmeans
```

Each row is a parameter, with its estimate (`mean`), standard error (`sd`) and
95% interval.

- `drift_stress` and `drift_mood` are the auto effects, per day. On its own,
  stress one unit above its equilibrium changes at a rate of about -0.5 units
  a day, and after one day about `exp(-0.54)`, or 0.58, of the deviation is
  left.
- `drift_mood_stress` is the effect of stress on mood: more stress lowers the
  rate of change of mood. `drift_stress_mood`, the effect of mood on stress,
  is small and its interval includes zero.
- `diff_stress` and `diff_mood` are the standard deviations of the random
  shocks. `diff_mood_stress` is a parameter for their correlation, and is not
  itself a correlation. The correlation is in
  `s$parmatrices` and `ctSummaryMatrices(fit)$estimate$DIFFUSIONcor`.
- `mvarstress` and `mvarmood` are the measurement error standard deviations.
- `mm_stress` and `mm_mood` are the average levels of the two variables, and
  `T0m_stress` and `T0m_mood` where the processes start relative to them.

The drift matrix as a whole decides whether the processes are stable and how
fast they change. They are stable when every eigenvalue has a negative real
part, and the eigenvalues give the time scale:

```{r drift}
est <- ctSummaryMatrices(fit)$estimate
est$DRIFT
eigen(est$DRIFT)$values
log(2) / abs(eigen(est$DRIFT)$values)    # half-lives, in days
```

Both eigenvalues are negative, and a disturbance to the system halves in one
and a half to two days.

How much people differ is in `popsd`, the standard deviations of the random
effects:

```{r popsd}
s$popsd
```

People differ in their typical stress by a standard deviation of about 0.7
and in their typical mood by about 0.5.

Since the data are simulated, the dynamic parameters can be set against the
values that generated them:

```{r truth}
pars <- c('drift_stress', 'drift_stress_mood', 'drift_mood_stress',
  'drift_mood', 'diff_stress', 'diff_mood', 'mvarstress', 'mvarmood')
data.frame(truth = c(-0.5, 0, -0.25, -0.3, 0.8, 0.6, 0.4, 0.4),
  s$popmeans[pars, c('mean', '2.5%', '97.5%')])
```

Every interval contains the generating value.

## Effects over time

A cross effect in a continuous time model is an effect on a rate of change.
The effect of stress on mood over a given time interval, the cross-lagged
coefficient a discrete time model would estimate, depends on the interval:

```{r discrete, fig.height = 4.4}
ctDiscretePars(fit, times = seq(0, 10, by = 0.1), plot = TRUE)
```

A unit of stress is followed by lower mood, most strongly two to three days
later, when the effect is about -0.2. `summary()` of
`ctDiscretePars(fit, times = ...)` gives the peaks and their times, and
`vignette('dynamics')` explains these curves.

## Individual trajectories

`ctPredict()` gives the model's predictions for each person over time. The
plot shows the observations, and lines for each person's expected values
given their earlier observations, with 95% intervals. The lines jump at each
observation, as it updates the prediction. `kalmanvec = 'ysmooth'` uses all of
a person's observations instead.

```{r predict, fig.height = 4.4}
ctPredict(fit, subjects = 1:2, plot = TRUE)
```

`ctSubjectPars()` gives each person's estimated parameters, here their own
typical levels and starting states. They are close to the levels that
generated the data:

```{r subjectpars}
sp <- ctSubjectPars(fit)
dim(sp)                     # draws x subjects x parameters
cor(sp[1, , 'mm_stress'], truelevels$mm_stress)
```

# A covariate

Age is in the data but not in the model. `ctScoreTest()` tests, without
refitting, whether a covariate would improve the model, and estimates the
effect it would have on each parameter:

```{r scoretest}
covariates <- unique(dat[, c('id', 'age')])
ctScoreTest(fit, covariates = covariates, tests = 'covariates')
```

Age affects the typical stress level, `mm_stress`, by about 0.3 per standard
deviation of age, and no other parameter stands out. In the model, a covariate is a time independent predictor
(`TIpredNames`), and its effects are given in the `tipreds` field of the
parameters it affects. With `tipredDefault = FALSE` it affects only those.

```{r model2}
model2 <- ctModel(LAMBDA = diag(2),
  manifestNames = c('stress', 'mood'), latentNames = c('stress', 'mood'),
  TIpredNames = 'age', tipredDefault = FALSE,
  MANIFESTMEANS = c('mm_stress, tipreds=c(age)', 'mm_mood'))
fit2 <- ctFit(dat, model2, cores = 2)
summary(fit2)$tipreds
anova(fit, fit2)
```

`ctPar()` writes such cell strings, with fields for a cell's transform, its
random effect and its covariate effects.

# Checking the model

`ctScoreTest()` also tests whether parameters the model holds fixed should
differ between people, whether the dynamics depend on the level of a process,
and whether cells fixed at zero should be free:

```{r check}
ctScoreTest(fit2)
```

Nothing stands out once the tests are adjusted for their number (`p_adj`).
`ctFitAdequacy()` tests the model's one-step-ahead predictions against the
data, and `ctModelImprove()` searches for a better model step by step.
`vignette('score-tests')` describes all three.
